newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to lift ban on Japan cars for WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to lift ban on Japan cars for WTO entry.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday it and Japan had agreed on liberalisation terms under which Taipei could join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), with Taiwan pledging to lift an long-standing ban on imported Japanese cars.
As a condition for joining the global trade group, Taiwan's Board of Foreign Trade would allow the import of 7,700 Japanese cars, the state-run Central News Agency said.
After meeting Japanese representatives, board director Lin Yi-fu said Taiwan would raise the annual quota to 10,000 cars after its entry into the WTO, the agency reported.
The agreement brought to 16 the number of countries that have completed bilateral WTO entry talks with Taiwan, a prerequisite for the island's admission.
Taiwan must still complete talks with 10 others, including the United States.
Taiwan and U.S. officials were engaged in their own bilateral talks in Taipei this week.
Taiwan's Board of Foreign Trade, a cabinet agency, pledged to further liberalise the economy to promote its drive for WTO membership.
"We not only will fulfil our pledge to open various markets after entry, but will also launch some liberalisation measures before entry," the board said.
Apart from the bilateral trade talks, Taiwan's WTO entry bid faces a formidable political obstacle because neighbouring China has said it should be granted membership first.

Beijing's entry bid picked up momentum after a major trade accord with Washington, but the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada have continued to block China's membership citing a range of trade barriers and poor legal protections.
At present, Taiwan bans direct imports of Japanese passenger cars in an effort to reduce its trade deficit with Japan, although Japanese manufacturers assemble cars in Taiwan.
Cars are one of Taiwan's most restricted industries, with the government maintaining high import tariffs to protect the island's 11 domestic carmakers.
In 1996, Taiwan agreed to allow the import of 7,000 South Korean cars in 1997, a total that also would rise after Taiwan enters the WTO.
